questions.text: Does a PUSH_N with N 1 to 3 add 1 to BUSY_CYCLES?
questions.default: Yes, 1 busy cycle per non-empty push.
questions.reason: The request fixes BUSY_CYCLES only for full words.
questions.answer: Yes. BUSY_CYCLES counts one per clock in which a push is processed, and that includes a PUSH_N with N from 1 to 3. Only a PUSH_N with N = 0 does not count.
questions.evidence: BUSY_CYCLES counts one per clock in which a push is processed (PUSH4 or PUSH_N with N>0), it is 32 bits and wraps; a PUSH_N with N = 0 does not count.
questions.risk_reason: no rule names it a behaviour, an interface or a cosmetic choice: treated as a cost choice

questions.text: Confirm the register map (offset, width, reset value and access of every register).
questions.default: The map given in registers.map, taken from the request tables, 32-bit registers.
questions.reason: Offsets are named in the request; confirm no others are needed.
questions.answer: Yes, with the map taken from the spec tables, not from a file called registers.map (the spec does not mention that file). All registers are 32 bits wide on 4-byte steps. 0x000 ID is RO and reads 0x20930001. 0x004 BUILD is RO and holds the USR_ACCESS word. 0x008 SCRATCH is RW and resets to 0. 0x010 CTRL is RW (bit 0 INIT, self-clearing) and resets to 0. 0x014 PUSH4 is WO. 0x018 PUSH_N is WO. 0x01C TAIL_LEN is RW, stores only bits 1:0 and resets to 0. 0x020 CRC is RO and reads 0x00000000 at reset (internal state 0xFFFFFFFF, final XOR applied on read). 0x024 BYTE_COUNT is RO and resets to 0. 0x028 BUSY_CYCLES is RO and resets to 0. Unmapped addresses read 0 and ignore writes. Writes to read-only registers are ignored.
questions.evidence: - Reset: CRC state is the start value 0xFFFFFFFF internally, so CRC reads 0x00000000 for no bytes (the final XOR is applied on read); BYTE_COUNT 0, BUSY_CYCLES 0, TAIL_LEN 0, CTRL 0.
questions.risk_reason: the register map is what host software and the test shell are written against

questions.text: This design has no reset input. Is every reset a reconfiguration of the FPGA (the device is reprogrammed, so every register starts from its initial value), or does something restart the running design (then it needs a reset input)?
questions.default: Every reset is a reconfiguration of the FPGA (reset model: reprogram): registers get initial values, control state included, and the design has no reset input. Record it in spec.yaml as reset: {model: reprogram}; a design that restarts while it runs is reset: {model: reset} with a reset port.
questions.reason: With no reset input, a register can start only from its initial value, which the FPGA loads at configuration (owner, 2026-11-26: particularly useful for designs whose every reset reprograms the device). A design that must restart while running needs a reset input and resets its control state; the two models are checked by different rules (STD-INIT-02).
questions.answer: No, the default does not hold. The design has a reset input: `rst`, active high, which is held for a few clocks at start. The core module `p3_crc_engine_core` has `rst` among its ports, and the reset values are specified (CRC state 0xFFFFFFFF, BYTE_COUNT 0, BUSY_CYCLES 0, TAIL_LEN 0, CTRL 0). The specification does not say whether reset can also be applied while the design is running, so I cannot settle that part.
questions.evidence: with ports `clk`, `rst` (active high), `h_we`, `h_re`, `h_addr[11:0]`, `h_wdata[31:0]`, `h_rdata[31:0]` and the design's own signals.
questions.risk_reason: a reset's polarity, style or value decides the start-up state and the interface

questions.text: Which verification profile should this run use? Profiles: prototype: fastest: lint and directed tests to V1; no coverage, no formal, no netlist checks; standard: today's default: V3 with the floors, constrained-random, bounded formal on the control logic, board smoke run; thorough: standard plus the netlist checks (functional simulation of the synthesised netlist, equivalence), 8 seeds, deeper formal; ip_release: thorough plus an independent spec bench, mutation floor 85, induction and PDR proofs, pyuvm bench: what a library 'verified' label needs; high_dependability: thorough plus the structures the interview chose (ECC, parity, safe FSM, TMR, watchdog) and fault-injection simulation; low_latency: standard plus the latency budget checks and the latency-path documentation rule. Answer with a profile name.
questions.reason: nothing in the spec asks for more or less; standard is the default and what runs today. measured on the development design: 9 s of checks against 9 s for standard (model time not included)
questions.risk_reason: a name, comment or ordering that is easy to change later

questions.text: Is this a production build that must be hard to copy, read back or debug? A yes turns on: readback security and JTAG access to the system monitor and the BSCAN block off, no debug core or debug port in the built design, and system-monitor alarms wired to a latched safe shutdown; the build then fails a gate for each of these that Vivado's own outputs do not show. Bitstream encryption and authentication are requested too, but on a Zynq MPSoC (the KR260) they are boot-image steps that are yours: the record lists them as handed over, never as done. You keep the key: the agent never makes, stores or programs one (eFUSE and BBRAM are yours). Answer yes or no.
questions.reason: nothing in the spec asks for a protected or production build. cost: not measured yet
